newsitem.title: UK: Arabs say summit failed, Europeans stress hopes.
newsitem.headline: Arabs say summit failed, Europeans stress hopes.

text.p: Arabs wrote off Washington's Middle East summit meeting as a failure on Thursday but Israel's European friends put their stress on calls for progress at resumed peace talks.
Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip were mostly quiet as the Islamic Resistance Movement prepared to mount mass protests against Israeli troops and settlers on Friday.

A Jewish settlers' leader in the West Bank, Pinchas Wallerstein, said he was preparing for the worst, believing frustrated Palestinians were likely to take again to the streets where 73 people died in riots sparked last week by the opening of an ancient tunnel under Jerusalem.
Norway, a key mediator in the Israel-Palestinian diplomatic breakthrough of 1993, said it was "very satisfied" that the parties have agreed to resume negotiations.
"Of course we would have liked to have seen more concrete results from Washington," said Norwegian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ingvard Havnen.
"Our expectations for the Washington summit were not high... From our view point it is very important that the Israeli withdrawal from Hebron is on the top of the agenda."

The Washington summit, attended by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and King Hussein of Jordan, ended on Wednesday without agreement on any of the substantial points the Arabs wanted settled.
Israel and the Palestinians agreed only to end violence and keep talking about matters the Palestinians thought they agreed with the Israelis a year ago.
Israel called the outcome a triumph and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said all sides had won.

But Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa declared: "It is clear that the Israelis did not come to Washington to make progress... The proposals submitted by the Israeli delegation constitute a total retreat from the framework of peace."
Hasan Asfour, a negotiator for Arafat's Palestine Liberation Organisation, said "the summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence."

Britain's Foreign Office said it was "essential that the two sides work for concrete and early results. Without real progress on the substance, there remains a grave threat to the whole peace process."
France welcomed the agreement to resume Israeli-Palestinian talks, adding that "only sincere implementation of existing accords will defeat the spiral of violence and relaunch the peace process."
Russia urged speed in the peace talks, and cautioned both sides again any actions on the ground that could touch off another explosion.
"The recent events in Jerusalem can be explained mostly by the measures taken by Israel," Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a news briefing in Moscow.
